name: Vegetarian Jajangmyeon
steps: Check the chunjang paste is free of animal-derived ingredients or seafood and the noodles are eggless. Peel and cut potatoes into 1 cm cubes. Cut zucchini, onion and mushrooms into similar small pieces so they cook evenly; cut the cucumber into thin matchsticks and keep it raw for serving.

Heat 20 ml neutral oil in a small pan over medium-low heat. Add the chunjang and stir constantly for 2–3 minutes until fragrant and glossy, without scorching; this reduces its raw bitterness. Scrape the fried paste into a bowl and set aside. The paste is salty, so do not add salt before tasting the finished sauce.

Heat the remaining 30 ml neutral oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Cook onion and mushrooms for 4 minutes, then add potato and zucchini and cook 4 minutes more, stirring often. Stir in the fried chunjang and sugar until all the vegetables are coated. Pour in 400 ml of the measured water, cover loosely and simmer for 10–12 minutes until the potato is tender.

Mix the cornstarch with the remaining 100 ml water allocated to the sauce, then stream it into the bubbling vegetables while stirring. Simmer for 1–2 minutes until the black sauce is thick and glossy; stir in sesame oil. Meanwhile boil the remaining 2000 ml water in a large pot, cook the eggless noodles as directed on the packet until springy, and drain well.

Divide noodles among four bowls and ladle one quarter of the hot black-bean vegetable sauce over each. Top with raw cucumber matchsticks and serve immediately; stir the sauce through the noodles at the table.
tips: Use Korean chunjang, not the Chinese yellow soybean paste used for Zhajiangmian; they give distinctly different sauces. Some chunjang products are pre-fried, so follow the package if it says ready to use. Keep the potato cubes small enough to cook through before thickening the sauce.
notes: Quantities serve four adults. Check the doneness cues in each step and adjust seasoning to taste. Jain suitability depends on your household ingredient rules.
